title: Personalization in the Era of LLMs - Shivam Verma, Spotify

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on fine-tuning open-weight LLMs with domain-specific catalog data, continual training with Semantic IDs, and parameter-efficient personalization via soft tokenization. Spotify is a media and content platform where recommendation drives engagement, while the underlying adaptation techniques generalize across domains. The talk covers both development of new adaptation techniques and their production deployment for podcast next-episode recommendations. Requires understanding of transformer architectures, embeddings, tokenization, auto-regressive generation, and fine-tuning methods. A conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer event. Multiple direct transcript quotes confirm fine-tuning, soft tokenization, Semantic ID tokenization, and production deployment.

summary: Shivam Verma from Spotify's AI foundation org presents on personalization in the era of LLMs. His team builds user embeddings and adapts open-weight LLMs for recommendations. The talk outlines three key components: foundational user modeling, content representation (teaching LLMs about the catalog), and combining both into a steerable personalized pipeline that goes from sequences of actions to vectors to tokens. Spotify has 750M MAUs, 100M+ tracks, ~400K audiobooks, millions of podcasts, video episodes, and operates in 184 markets. Current products include Discover Weekly (since 2015), AI DJ, prompted playlists (now supporting podcasts), and a taste profile feature (in limited markets, expanding later this year) that lets users see and control what Spotify knows about them. Historically, Spotify used traditional recommender systems ("trad wrecks") with multi-stage pipelines: candidate generation reducing millions to hundreds, then ranking stages, with separate teams and models per product surface. The company is now moving toward a single unified model with an LLM backbone. User embeddings are generated daily for over a billion users, making it a massive, expensive pipeline. The approach has evolved from autoencoder-based user representations to a single sequential transformer model that takes user interactions as context alongside request context, query, product surface, and candidate items. A visualization from a newer model shows cross-content modeling where users, tracks (blue), and podcast episodes (pink) are embedded in the same space. For catalog understanding, Spotify uses Semantic IDs — compressing high-dimensional content vectors into 4-6 tokens in a hierarchical structure, where shared initial tokens capture broad categories (e.g., both Ariana Grande and Bruno Mars share their first two tokens as pop artists) and later tokens capture niche distinctions. Open-weight LLMs like Llama or Gwen are continually trained with this catalog data, enabling auto-regressive generation of the next song or episode as the next token in a sequence. Tradeoffs include catastrophic forgetting, but the models effectively combine world knowledge with Spotify's platform knowledge. For personalization, user embeddings are projected into the LLM's token space as a soft token, giving the frozen model a user-specific token to attend over. This avoids full fine-tuning on all 750M users while enabling per-user personalization. Podcast next-episode recommendations are already productionized on this stack, with positive internal metrics. The taste profile product lets users chat or send messages to edit what Spotify knows about them, feeding those edits back into the generative model.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and talk scope
sections.summary: Shivam Verma introduces himself as tech lead of the user representations team in Spotify's AI foundation org. The talk focuses on context engineering on the modeling side rather than agentic context engineering, covering how Spotify uses user data for recommendations. His background is in machine learning, previously at Twitter, based in London.

sections.title: Three pillars of personalization
sections.summary: Outlines three key aspects: foundational user modeling (understanding users), content side (teaching LLMs about the catalog), and combining both into something steerable and personalized. The pipeline conceptually goes from sequences of actions to vectors to tokens, then combines them with an LLM.

sections.title: Spotify scale and personalization products
sections.summary: Spotify has 750M MAUs, 100M+ tracks, ~400K audiobooks, millions of podcasts, video episodes, and operates in 184 markets. Products include Discover Weekly (since 2015), AI DJ, prompted playlists (now supporting podcasts), and taste profile (few markets, expanding later this year) that exposes what Spotify knows about users and lets them control it.

sections.title: From traditional recommenders to unified models
sections.summary: Describes 'trad wrecks' — traditional multi-stage recommender pipelines with candidate generation reducing millions to hundreds, then ranking stages, with separate teams and models per product surface. Spotify is moving toward a single unified model with an LLM backbone that users can steer.

sections.title: User embeddings at scale
sections.summary: User embeddings represent user taste across all historical sessions and form the foundation for all downstream models. Generated daily for over a billion users, the pipeline is massive and expensive. The approach has evolved from autoencoder-based representations (compressing/decompressing features) to sequential transformer models that take user interactions as context alongside request context, query, product surface, and items.

sections.title: Cross-content embedding visualization
sections.summary: Shows a visualization from a newer model embedding users (green), tracks (blue), and podcast episodes (pink) in the same space on a hypersphere. The speaker's embedding is close to big tech podcasts, demonstrating cross-content modeling where users live alongside content in a shared space, enabling exploration of taste neighborhoods.

sections.title: Catalog understanding and Semantic IDs
sections.summary: Explains catalog understanding: training vectors to represent items (songs, artists, podcasts, episodes), combining Spotify's platform knowledge with world knowledge from open-weight LLMs (Llama, Gwen). Semantic IDs compress high-dimensional content vectors into 4-6 tokens, analogous to word tokenization, enabling LLMs to autoregressively generate the next song or episode. Tradeoffs include catastrophic forgetting, but models effectively combine world and platform knowledge for recommendations.

sections.title: Semantic ID examples and training approach
sections.summary: Demonstrates Semantic IDs with Ariana Grande and Bruno Mars, each represented as six token IDs. The first two tokens are shared because both are pop artists; remaining tokens capture niche distinctions in a hierarchical structure. LLMs are continually trained with Spotify catalog data using Semantic IDs, teaching them to 'talk with semantic IDs.' An example shows an Italian user's listening history tokenized and used as training data to predict the next episode, with Spotify URIs converted to Semantic ID tokens the model attends over.

sections.title: Assembling a steerable personalized generative recommender
sections.summary: Describes assembling all components into a single steerable personalized generative recommender. The taste profile product lets users chat or send messages to edit what Spotify knows about them, with edits flowing back into the generative model. Since models cannot be trained on all 750M+ users, collaborative filtering provides generalization while soft tokenization provides personalization: user embeddings are projected into the LLM's token space as a soft token, giving the frozen model a user-specific token to attend over.

sections.title: Results and production deployment
sections.summary: Reports positive early results on internal metrics. Podcast next-episode recommendations are already productionized on this stack. Summarizes the three components: embeddings representing users, Semantic IDs representing compressed content, and soft tokenization projecting users into the model's token space. This moves away from traditional recommender systems toward sequential modeling, which Spotify is excited to expand across all recommender surfaces.
